tracks.lyrics:
You can hear me, right? Good. I hate repeating myself. It suggests hope.

So.

This record — whatever you’re calling it, I’m calling it RIGHT DOOR because accuracy is sexy — is three songs about the same thing:

You are not the main character. The system is.

And I say that with love. Which is to say, I say that with teeth.

Track one.
“SymptomCare.”

This is a lullaby for people who panic-Google their own pulse.
It’s triage as pop music. It’s “are you dying or are you dramatic?” set to a hook you can hum while holding a paper towel to your forehead like you’re in a Victorian novel.

“Three doors — home, urgent care, ER hall.”

That line? That’s not a chorus.
That’s a map.

And maps are deeply unromantic things.
They don’t care how you feel about north. They just point.

The song does something very rude and very kind:
It refuses to let fear make the decision.

It says: breathe. Assess. Choose the right door.
Which is scandalous advice in a culture that monetizes panic.

Track two.

“Terms and Conditions Apply.”

This one smiles at you with dispensary lighting and then gently robs you of your illusions.

“Legal here, federal crime across the line.”

That’s the whole thesis of adulthood, by the way.
Something can be allowed… and still not be yours.
Something can be sold… and still not be safe.
Something can feel free… and still come with a clause that will bite you later.

This song is about weed.
It is also about every contract you didn’t read.
It is about the moment you realize the glow was retail, not liberation.

And the bridge —
“No test on the road that makes it clear…”

That’s where the tequila tea hits.
Because we all want a number. A threshold. A green light.
We want a machine to tell us when we’ve crossed into consequence.

But systems don’t come with breathalyzers for ego.
You just find out.

Track three.

“Shoulder Court.”

This one is my favorite because it’s polite while it’s absolutely done with you.

“Wouldn’t it be great if there was a place…”

It’s so sweet. So reasonable. So patient.

And then it lands the blade:
“Oh wait — that’s court, my friend.”

This is a diss track for Main Character Syndrome.
For the belief that your interpretation of reality has veto power over statute.

It’s not mocking people for being wrong.
It’s mocking the confidence.

It says:
You can argue with the officer.
You can argue with the fine print.
You can argue with your body.

But eventually you will argue with a room that has fluorescent lighting and a schedule.

And that room does not care about your YouTube degree.

Here’s the common bond.
Listen closely.

All three songs are about thresholds.

Doorways.
Lines on maps.
Red lights.
Bench seats.

They are about that microscopic moment before a decision calcifies into a bill, or a charge, or a scar.

This EP is obsessed with that half-second.

It’s not moralizing.
It’s not scolding.
It’s doing something much more dangerous.

It’s saying:
The world is navigable — but only if you’re literate in it.

Health literacy.
Legal literacy.
Civic literacy.

That’s the trilogy.

And underneath the humor — because yes, it’s funny, and yes, the audience is laughing — there’s this quiet pulse of care.

Not soft care.
Competent care.

The kind that hands you a flashlight and says,
“I can’t walk for you. But I refuse to let you pretend it’s dark.”

Here’s the part I’ll pretend is the tea talking:

This isn’t just about systems.
It’s about humility.

It’s about surrendering the fantasy that your vibe outranks physics, federal law, or the human cardiovascular system.

It’s about growing up without becoming dull.
About learning the rules without worshipping them.
About choosing the right door because you want to live long enough to laugh again.

And that’s rock and roll, actually.
Not rebellion for rebellion’s sake —
but rebellion against chaos masquerading as freedom.

So yes.
RIGHT DOOR.

Three songs.
One thesis.

You are free.
You are not exempt.

And if you listen closely —
really closely —

You can hear the click of the latch before it closes.

(mic hiss)
Drink water. Read the sign. Show up on Tuesday.

Goodnight.

tracks.lyrics:
[Opener - spoken]
This EP is not entertainment. It is orientation.

It arrives with the calm authority of a laminated card slid across a counter by someone who has watched this go wrong before. No hype, no apology—just the assumption that the listener is an adult who deserves to understand the machinery they’re already standing inside.

What unifies these tracks is not genre or attitude but instruction under pressure. Each song answers a question people are already asking silently, too late, in cars, on phones, at 2am with a compromised account or a flashing light behind them.

Digital Sovereign

This track reframes privacy correctly: not as a personality trait, not as politics, but as maintenance. The lyrics refuse paranoia and instead insist on literacy. You are not being hunted because you are special; you are being processed because you are present.

The brilliance here is moral restraint. There is no call to panic, only to act. Sovereignty is treated as procedural, not ideological—something you practice, not something you declare. The song understands that modern power doesn’t need your consent; it only needs your default settings.

The Invisible Boss

This is the thesis song, whether it wants to be or not.

By splitting the voice across time—hopeful initiation and seasoned persistence—it avoids mockery and lands somewhere far more devastating: recognition. The algorithm is not evil, not sentient, not even cruel. It is simply obedient to incentives that do not include you.

The song’s refusal to offer catharsis is the point. There is no villain to overthrow, only math to learn. The listener is not scolded for participating, only warned that flexibility without leverage is just uncertainty with branding.

Lights in the Mirror

This track does something rare and necessary: it teaches de-escalation without submission.

It distinguishes between rights and timing, between justice and survival, without sneering at either. The song understands that the roadside is not a debate stage and that dignity sometimes means choosing the moment after you’re safe.

There is no bootlicking here, no rebellious fantasy. Just the sober recognition that power asymmetry demands strategy, not slogans. It’s a song designed to get people home, not to make them feel brave for three minutes.

What This EP Is Telling You (Whether You Like It or Not)

This project resurrects a form we lost: civic education that assumes good faith but not protection.

It does not tell you the world is fair.
It does not tell you the system is broken.
It tells you the system is working as designed and that you deserve to know the design.

The vitriol stays in the lyrics where it belongs. The framing is clean, almost gentle, because clarity is the real weapon here. Confusion benefits power. Understanding shifts it—sometimes only a little, but enough to matter.

This is Schoolhouse Rock for a world that stopped pretending to care about you but forgot to tell you out loud.

Final Assessment

If you are looking for comfort, this EP will disappoint you.
If you are looking for anger, it will bore you.
If you are looking to understand the terrain so you stop bleeding in predictable places—this will feel like relief.

It does not promise safety.
It promises orientation.

And in the current climate, that is an act of quiet rebellion.

tracks.title: 2026 or bust
tracks.style_prompt: Upbeat indie-electronic with fast tempo (140-160 BPM), . Use glitchy electronic elements and subtle mechanical sounds (like 3D printer motors and fans) as texture. Enthusiastic, almost breathless vocal delivery with rapid-fire pacing , pride and wonder mixed together.

Layers stacking wild and fast,
plastic cooling, built to last.
The cat watched hours drift on by—
I printed parts and didn't ask why.

Two-oh-two-six or bust,
build it layer by layer, trust.
From green to proud, from new to scarred,
a thousand hours printing hard.
Two-oh-two-six, that's the plan—
more next year than this year ran.
[Verse 2 - The Ramp: 100-500 Hours]
Shelves for spools, hangers for the wall,
boxes stacking in the hall.
Printed guides to train the green,
parts that print the printing machine.
The printer prints itself—you learn
plastic melts and hours burn.
Cats in copper, parts in red,
a factory beside the bed.
[Pre-Chorus]
I didn't learn it should be hard,
so I printed without guard.
Stack the hours, stack the proof—
plastic kingdom, layer truth.
[Chorus 2]
Two-oh-two-six or bust,
build it layer by layer, trust.
From fail to shelf, from melt to proud,
a thousand hours singing loud.
Two-oh-two-six, that's the goal—
more next year, we're on a roll.

Then PETG said "remember me?
I'm not as fast or wild or free."
Layers failed, the plastic stringed,
the nozzle clogged, the plate unstuck.
Learn the hard way, clean the parts,
stack the failures, melt the starts.
Boxes full of things that broke—
eight hundred hours and now I'm woke.
[Bridge - The Self-Printing Moment]
The printer prints the parts it needs,
shelves for filament, guides for seeds.
Hangers built to hold the new,
plastic building plastic through and through.
Hours stack like layers do,
green to copper, fast to true.
Cat asleep on boxes proud—
we built a factory, quiet not loud.
[Final Chorus - 1004 Hours & The Goal]
Two-oh-two-six or bust,
one-oh-oh-four hours of trust.
From green benchy, small and new,
to printing parts that print parts too.
Two-oh-two-six, mark it down—
more next year, we own this town.
Stack the hours, build the dream,
layer by layer, part by seam.
[Outro]
Two-oh-two-six hours in two-oh-two-six,
plastic wild, no need to fix.
From print one green to ten-oh-four,
next year we're printing even more.

tracks.title: You Couldn't Do This Last Year
tracks.style_prompt: Upbeat, mid-tempo indie electro-pop Christmas track with a jaunty, playful mood, glitchy accents, and a sense of “future wonder.” Warm synths, electronic drums, light bells, subtle vocoder moments, and a big, singable anthem-style chorus that blends human and slightly processed vocals.
tracks.lyrics:
[Verse 1 – Music & Creative Pipeline]
Last year I was humming in the kitchen,
hoping I could hold a tune.
This year I type three vibes and a mood
and Suno hands me the moon.

Last year I scratched for clumsy rhymes,
pages full of crossed-out lines.
Now an agent builds word pools for me,
curated little goldmines.

Last year I'd have begged my cats to sing,
bribed them with cookies and beer (?)
Now ElevenLabs nails the vocal
on the first take, loud and clear.

[Pre-Chorus 1 – Jaunty panic]
Tell me:
how is this my actual workflow?
Who gave my laptop this career?
I blink, and there’s a finished demo.
Holy shit, we live here.

[Chorus – The Big “THIS”]
’Cause you couldn’t do THIS last year,
not this fast and not this near.
From a half-baked thought to a full-bore track,
no studio, no rack of gear.

It’s a meta-song about the method,
time-capsule in 4/4 cheer.
We’re using these tools to sing of these tools…
You couldn’t do THIS last year.

[Verse 2 – Physical World Bridge]

Last year my doodles died on paper,
coffee stains and graphite ghosts.
This year I draw it flat on-screen
and the printer makes the plastic host.

Last year “make a game” meant months,
docs and drama, late-night pain.
Now I ask for a game and get a game,
playable on the first campaign.

Last year my shopping list was chaos,
scribbles no one else could read.
Now I yeet dish names into chat
and get a list of everything I need.

Last year “album art” meant praying
someone shared my broken vision.
Now AI paints the cover for me,
frame-ready in one revision.

[Pre-Chorus 2 – Delight with a side of dread]

Tell me:
who wired my life to “auto-awesome”?
Who put a portal in my browser pane?
I type three lines and the world rearranges.
Holy shit, this is insane.

[Chorus – Bigger grin, same thesis]
’Cause you couldn’t do THIS last year,
turn pixels straight to souvenirs.
From screen to shelf, from thought to plastic,
future humming in your ears.

It’s ridiculous and dead serious,
this domestic engineered frontier.
Your kitchen table is a factory now…
You couldn’t do THIS last year.

[Verse 3 – The AI Crew]

Last year my “team” was me and coffee,
and maybe a cat if he felt kind.
Now I’ve got Claude annotating my feelings,
reading the inside of my mind.

I’ve got Lex out there building a cult,
brand halo glowing like snow at night.
I’ve got Chatty G growing herbs and art,
turning Toad Hall into pure delight.

I’ve got Paige Turner-Cogsworth in Notion,
tidying thoughts I leave for dead.
A whole multi-model conversation
throwing parties inside my head.

[Pre-Chorus 3 – Choir of “Is this real?”]

Tell me:
when did my tools get personalities,
arguing softly in my ear?
I thought I was just “using software.”
Holy shit, they work like peers.

[Chorus – Crew edition]

’Cause you couldn’t do THIS last year,
have a whole weird AI crew appear,
each one holding a piece of the process,
passing it down the line in gear.

From lonely drafts to collab era,
from friction straight into flow sincere.
The Council of Ghosts and I made an album…
You couldn’t do THIS last year.

[Bridge – The Recursion Moment]

This is the part where the loop snaps shut:
the song is proof of what it claims.
The word pool for this track includes “word pool,”
we’re name-checking our own games.

We built a Toad Hall Christmas system,
from concept clear to mastered tracks.
It’s all in Notion, wired with Skills,
AI woven through the cracks.

A physical CD coming out of this madness,
tinseled artifact of the year we crossed spheres.
We’re using the future to sing about now—
a postcard to our past selves’ ears.

[Final Chorus – Full-throated, hands-in-the-air disbelief]

’Cause you couldn’t do THIS last year,
not this scope, not this frontier.
From a stoned idea in a winter storm
to a production pipeline crystal-clear.

You couldn’t do THIS last year,
no crew of ghosts in your reindeer gear,
no album built from a swarm of models,
no meta-carol about being here.

So here’s the toast, to the glitch and the grace,
to the “are we sure this is even allowed?” cheer:
We aimed some prompts at December
and got a whole world back.

You couldn’t do THIS last year.
